iṣṭāpūrta
(‘what is sacrificed and what is filled’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘iṣṭāpūrta’ is very ancient. It has been used in the Ṛgveda (10.14.8), the Atharvaveda (3.29.1), the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (7.7.1-3) as also in some of the major उपनिषद्स् like the Kaṭha (1.8) and the Muṇḍaka (

iṣṭi
(‘sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices are classified into several groups. One group in which there are four priests अध्वर्यु, आग्नीध्र, होतृ and ब्रह्मन् and the material used for oblation is आज्य (clarified butter) or पुरोडाश (rice-cake) or चरु (porridge), is called an ‘iṣṭi’.
The Darśa and the Pūrṇamāsa are the models for an इष्टि.
The word is also used to indicate a particular mode of offering oblation as different from आहुति and होम.
See also DARŚAPŪRṆAMĀSA and VEDIC SACRIFICES.

iṣṭakā
(‘burnt brick’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices often need a proper alter which is normally made of burnt bricks. Such bricks, made of clay, must be as long as the length of the foot of the yajamāna or the sacrificer. Three lines are also drawn on them.
The total number needed for the altars of some sacrifices (in five layers) is 10,800.
The very first brick prepared by the wife of the sacrificer is named āṣāḍhā. Three more prepared by the sacrificer himself are called ‘viśvajyotis’. Other types of bricks are also named with such special nomenclature as yajuṣmatī, lokampṛṇā, vālakhilyā, svayamātṛṇṇā, citriṇī and so on. They are used in different parts of the altar structure, with appropriate mantras known as iṣṭakāmantras.
See also VEDIC SACRIFICES.

Iṣṭasiddhi
(‘attaining what is desired’)
------------------------------------------
Vedānta in general, and Advaita Vedānta in particular, has two aspects: statement of its theories and dialectical demolition of other schools. Among the latter group of works, the Iṣṭasiddhi of विमुक्तात्मन् (circa A.

) has earned for itself an important place. It is the fourth work in the Siddhi category, the other three being Brahmasiddhi, Naiṣkarmyasiddhi and Advaitasiddhi, of मण्डन मिश्र (8th cent. A. D.), सुरेश्वर (8th century A. D.) and मधुसूदन सरस्वती (A.

-1632) respectively.
The Iṣṭasiddhi has been considered as such an extremely important polemical work of Advaita Vedānta that it has been accepted as an authority by later writers, not only of Advaita but also of other schools.
The work devotes a major part to the analysis of the various theories of error (called ‘khyāti’) and shows their defects. It defends the anirvacanīyakhyāti of the Advaita Vedānta. It establishes the inexplicable character of the world of māyā.
As regards the removal of अविद्या or nescience, it puts forward its own theory as the fifth mode (pañcamaprakāra). Since अविद्या is अनिर्वचनीय or indescribable, its removal also is अनिर्वचनीय!
Even in जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation while alive), विमुक्तात्मन् feels, there is a trace of इग्नोरन्चे (avidyāleśa); because, the continuance of vyavahāra (day-to-day activities) is impossible without a certain degree of attachment to the body and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the external world as a separate entity.
Advaitins attribute two other views to विमुक्तात्मन्; that there are as many knowledges as there are nesciences; that the आत्मन् binds itself and also releases itself.
The entire work is in the form of kārikās or verses and explanations in prose.
Jñānottama (10th century A. D.) has written a commentary called Vivaraṇa.

iṣṭaliṅga
(‘liṅga dear to one’)
------------------------------------------
Vīraśaivism, one of the several aspects of शैविस्म्, has prescribed a special mode of दीक्षा or initiation. The गुरु gives triple दीक्षा to the disciple. Kriyādīkṣā, the first, has a ceremonial form in which the गुरु gives the disciple a लिङ्ग (emblem of शिव, usually of stone, but encased in a silver casket) after worshipping it. The disciple has to wear it like a necklace. He has to worship it thrice daily—in the morning, at noon and in the evening.
Even women can receive such a दीक्षा and can perform its worship.
For one who has received the लिङ्ग there is no need to observe अशौच or ceremonial impurity.
It is this लिङ्ग that is called ‘iṣṭaliṅga’.
The other two aspects of दीक्षा are mantradīkṣā (imparting the famous मन्त्र, namaś śivāya) and vedadīkṣā (infusing knowledge by direct contact).
See also ŚAIVISM.

iṣṭadevatā
(‘deity [of contemplation] dear to oneself ’)
------------------------------------------
Though God is one, his aspects for contemplation can be many. The path of भक्ति gives the freedom to the spiritual aspirants to choose any of these aspects for the purpose of meditation. Any one of these aspects which the aspirant chooses, becomes his ‘iṣṭadevatā’ (chosen deity dear to oneself).
The general rule is that the aspirant has to stick to one इष्टदेवता. He should receive and repeat one मन्त्र pertaining to it till he gets realisation. For this he should have only one गुरु or spiritual teacher.
In traditional initiation, the गुरु generally gives the मन्त्र along with certain ritualistic instructions like nyāsas (purificatory processes), dhyānaśloka (hymn of contemplation) and the मन्त्र in which the बीज (seed letter) is imbedded.
See also BHAKTIYOGA.
